article.overview: A lunar surface observatory is an astronomical instrument, or a small set of instruments, placed on the Moon's surface to observe the sky. The name describes a payload class rather than one design: a surface observatory may be an ultraviolet camera, an ultraviolet telescope, an X-ray detector or a radio antenna array. Its appeal comes from the lunar setting. The Moon has an extremely thin exosphere, so the light observed is not absorbed or blurred by a thick atmosphere, and the lunar far side is proposed for radio cosmology experiments [4]. Against these advantages, a surface observatory must survive about two weeks of lunar night, large temperature swings and lunar dust, and it depends on a lander or rover for delivery. This article discusses four flown examples and one example still in development. The evidence for each differs in strength: the Apollo 16 and Chang'e-3 LUT descriptions rest on primary or agency-linked records, while several mass, dimension and operating-status claims rest on secondary reporting and are flagged as such.
article.description: A surface observatory has four functional parts. First, a collecting element (a Schmidt camera, a telescope mirror, an X-ray collimator or an antenna) gathers the signal. Second, a detector or receiver turns the signal into a record: photographic film with electronographic amplification in the Apollo 16 camera [2], a cooled ultraviolet-enhanced CCD in the Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (LUT) [3], a single-pixel photon counter in the Lunokhod 1 RT-1 X-ray instrument [9], and a spectrometer connected to antennas in LuSEE-Night [4]. Third, a pointing or orientation arrangement sets the field of view: a flat mirror on a two-axis gimbal in LUT [3], a rover-mounted instrument that scanned the sky in strips as the Moon rotated [9], fixed imagers on the ILO-X lander [5], and a turntable for the LuSEE-Night antennas [4]. Fourth, the observatory needs power, thermal control, data storage and a communication path. A surface observatory is therefore as much a lander or rover engineering task as an optical or radio design. Data may also wait a long time before reaching Earth: the LuSEE-Night team expects about 40 days before its first dataset is relayed by satellite [4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Surface observatories are used to observe sources that are difficult to study from Earth. Ultraviolet work is the best-documented area so far. The Apollo 16 camera was designed for far-ultraviolet observations of the Earth's outer atmosphere (the geocorona), stars and nebulae, and on 22 April 1972 it recorded the Large Magellanic Cloud over 1050 to 1600 angstroms [1][2]. LUT on Chang'e-3 was designed for near-ultraviolet imaging of the sky, and its authors reported more than 130,000 images by the end of December 2014 [3]. The Lunokhod 1 RT-1 instrument was an X-ray telescope that scanned the sky in strips as the rover's zenith-pointed field of view moved with lunar rotation [9]. Radio work is the main long-term goal of LuSEE-Night: to show that the far side can host radio cosmology experiments and, as a stretch goal, to detect the cosmic Dark Ages signal directly [4]. The ILO-X imagers were a lander-mounted imaging experiment for the lunar surface and descent, and reported first images include surface, regolith, the Sun and the lander itself [5][6].
article.operating_principle: The Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera was an F/1, 3-inch Schmidt camera. It operated in a dual spectroscopic and direct-view mode, and its image was recorded on nuclear emulsion film after electronographic amplification, with a film transport mechanism [2]. The Chang'e-3 LUT is a 150 mm Ritchey-Chretien telescope with a focal ratio of F/3.75 and a two-lens field corrector. A flat pointing mirror on a two-dimensional gimbal points and tracks targets, and the image falls on a UV-enhanced CCD at the Nasmyth focus [3]. Its near-ultraviolet throughput peaks at 2500 angstroms, at about 8 per cent, with an effective full width at half maximum of 1080 angstroms [3]. The Lunokhod 1 RT-1 had no grazing-incidence optics. Its field of view of about 3 degrees was set by a metallic grid, and lunar rotation moved that field across the sky [9]. The ILO-X imagers are fixed colour (Bayer-filter) cameras: a wide field of 186 degrees full angle and a narrow field of 39 by 51 degrees [5]. LuSEE-Night is a radio instrument with four antennas about three metres long, deployed from a turntable, with a spectrometer as its core [4].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar surface observatories matter because they test whether the Moon can host long-duration astronomy, and because some wavelengths are hard to observe from Earth's surface. Ultraviolet light is absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, so an ultraviolet telescope on the Moon can observe bright sources without that absorption and can monitor them over long periods [3]. The far side has been proposed for radio observations at very long wavelengths, where Earth-based work is constrained by interference and by the ionosphere; the LuSEE-Night team presents its mission as a test of whether the far side can support radio cosmology [4]. The early instruments are historically important as the first attempts at astronomy from a lunar surface. Their scientific return, however, is uneven. The Apollo 16 observations were short [10], the LUT photometric stability is described only qualitatively in the primary paper [3], and the scientific yield of the Lunokhod 1 RT-1 and the ILO-X images has not been reviewed in detail for this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, power or optical specification for a lunar surface observatory. The examples below range from a 1970 X-ray instrument and a 1972 film camera, through a 2013 CCD telescope and a 2024 commercial-lander imager, to a radio array in development. They are not directly comparable: a 150 mm telescope, a three-metre radio antenna array and a sub-kilogram imager answer different questions. Where a figure is not in a primary or verified source, it is marked as not publicly specified.

examples.name: Lunokhod 1 RT-1 X-ray telescope
examples.status: Flown on the Moon, 1970 (secondary sources only)
examples.description: RT-1 (Roentgen Telescope-1) was carried on the Soviet Lunokhod 1 rover. It was a single-pixel X-ray photon counter with a field of view restricted to about 3 degrees by a metallic grid, and it did not use grazing-incidence optics. It was mounted to point at the zenith, so lunar rotation scanned the sky in strips, and it observed during at least three lunar days [9]. The rover was intended to operate through three lunar days and is reported to have operated for eleven [9]. Sources differ on the end of operations. Mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources read for this article, and the scientific results of RT-1 have not been checked against primary publications.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in sources read
examples.optics_or_receiver: Single-pixel X-ray photon counter; metallic grid collimation to about 3 degrees; no grazing-incidence optics

examples.name: Apollo 16 Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph
examples.description: The instrument was built at the Naval Research Laboratory under George Carruthers and flown on Apollo 16 [2]. Its primary collecting system is an F/1, 3-inch Schmidt camera, and it operated in a dual spectroscopic and direct-view mode. The image was recorded on nuclear emulsion film after electronographic amplification, with a film transport mechanism [2]. Page and Carruthers report imaging over 1050 to 1600 angstroms and spectra over 900 to 1600 angstroms, and an observation of the Large Magellanic Cloud on 22 April 1972 at about 3 arc-minute resolution [1]. The Smithsonian record gives an overall size of 49.5 by 78.7 by 53.3 cm, but that object is a reconstructed back-up engineering model (serial number 4), not the flown unit [2]. A secondary encyclopaedia-derived source gives a mass of 22 kg, a 75 mm f/1.0 optic, a 20-degree imaging field, and placement in the lunar module's shadow to limit heating and glare [10]. These values have not been checked against a primary NASA document. The film transport mechanism is documented as having returned to Earth, but the primary record does not say whether the rest of the camera was left on the surface [2].
examples.mass_source_note: Secondary source only [10]; not verified against NASA primary documents
examples.dimensions: 49.5 x 78.7 x 53.3 cm for a reconstructed back-up model (not the flown unit); axis labels not stated
examples.optics_or_receiver: F/1, 3-inch Schmidt camera; electronographic amplification onto nuclear emulsion film

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Lunar-based Ultraviolet Telescope (LUT)
examples.status: Flown on the Moon; launched 2 December 2013; first light 16 December 2013
examples.description: LUT is a 150 mm aperture, F/3.75 Ritchey-Chretien telescope. A flat pointing mirror on a two-axis gimbal points and tracks targets, and a two-lens field corrector with a near-ultraviolet coating sits in front of the focal plane [3]. The detector is a UV-enhanced e2v CCD with 13 micrometre pixels and 1024 by 1024 active pixels at the Nasmyth focus. It can be cooled to about 40 degrees C below ambient, and science images were taken at -40 degrees C [3]. The field of view is 1.36 by 1.36 square degrees. Throughput peaks at 2500 angstroms, at about 8 per cent, with an effective FWHM of 1080 angstroms, and two 286 nm LEDs provide an internal flat field [3]. The telescope was launched on 2 December 2013 and achieved first light on 16 December 2013 [3]. The authors report more than 130,000 images by the end of December 2014, and describe photometric performance over the first six months as highly stable, without a numerical stability figure in the text read [3]. Mass, power, limiting magnitude and lander mounting are not stated in that paper [3]. A 2017 report, which is secondary, describes LUT as still operational [11]. That status was not confirmed from a primary source for this article.
examples.optics_or_receiver: Ritchey-Chretien telescope; gimbal-mounted flat pointing mirror; two-lens field corrector; UV-enhanced e2v CCD, 1024 x 1024 pixels, 13 micrometre pixels, cooled to -40 degrees C for science
examples.wavelength_band: Near-ultraviolet; throughput peak 2500 angstroms (about 8 per cent), effective FWHM 1080 angstroms

examples.name: ILO-X imagers (wide-field imager later named Lunar Codex)
examples.status: Flown on Intuitive Machines IM-1 (Nova-C), landed 22 February 2024; post-landing status not confirmed
examples.description: The ILO-X payload comprised two fixed imagers on the Nova-C IM-1 lander. The planning article gives the wide-field imager as circular with a 186-degree full-angle field, about 0.06 degrees per pixel, and a 3000-pixel-diameter Bayer-colour image. The narrow-field imager has a 39 by 51 degree field, about 0.013 degrees per pixel and 3000 by 4000 Bayer-colour pixels. Both are fixed with no moving parts, carry 32 GB of onboard memory each, and have optics designed for -180 degrees C to +70 degrees C [5]. Aperture is reported as 3 cm for each camera and the instrument mass as about 0.6 kg in ILOA-linked reporting [6]. The primary planning page does not state aperture, mass or power [5]. The imagers sat about 4.5 m above the surface, on a lander 4.3 m tall with a 1,908 kg launch mass, about 130 kg surface payload and 200 W of solar power on the surface [5]. ILOA reports a first surface image on 25 February 2024 and a descent frame about 4.2 minutes before touchdown [6]. Reports describe the lander as off-nominal, with the imagers still mounted near its top [6]. The planned surface life was nearly two weeks [5]. The wide-field imager was later renamed Lunar Codex [6]. Operating status after early 2024 was not confirmed for this article.
examples.dimensions: Not stated in primary planning page
examples.optics_or_receiver: Two fixed Bayer-colour imagers, no moving parts; 32 GB onboard memory each; optics designed for -180 to +70 degrees C
examples.field_of_view: Wide: circular, 186 degrees full angle, about 0.06 degrees per pixel. Narrow: 39 x 51 degrees, about 0.013 degrees per pixel

examples.name: LuSEE-Night radio observatory
examples.status: In development in the sources reviewed; launch not confirmed
examples.description: LuSEE-Night is a NASA and DOE radio experiment in development. It deploys four three-metre antennas, developed by Berkeley Lab, on a turntable, and its spectrometer is described as the heart of the instrument [4]. The battery-powered design has a strict mass limit, but no figure is given [4]. NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme coordinates the launch [4]. After touchdown, the lander shuts off permanently so that it does not cause interference, and the antennas then deploy [4]. The stated design life is two years of data collection, and survival of the first lunar night is the main open question [4]. A secondary summary gives a frequency range below 50 MHz [7], but the primary article gives no frequency numbers [4]. The carrier has been reported as Firefly's Blue Ghost lander [8], and a late-2026 launch was reported in a secondary talk-page summary [7]. Neither was confirmed against a current primary schedule, and the 2023 article gives no launch date [4].
examples.mass_note: Strict mass limit stated, no figure given
examples.dimensions: Four three-metre antennas on a turntable
examples.optics_or_receiver: Four antennas (three metres each) with a spectrometer; battery-powered

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are available for only a few examples, and not on a common basis. The Apollo 16 record gives an overall size of 49.5 by 78.7 by 53.3 cm for a display back-up model, with the axes not labelled [2]. The LUT telescope aperture is 150 mm [3]. The ILO-X imagers are small fixed units mounted about 4.5 m above the surface on the lander [5]. The LuSEE-Night antennas are each about three metres long [4]. The enclosure dimensions of RT-1 and the LuSEE-Night electronics are not publicly specified in the sources read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass values are sparse and come from different types of source. The Apollo 16 camera is given as 22 kg in a secondary source [10], while the primary Smithsonian record states no mass [2]. The ILO-X instruments are reported at about 0.6 kg in ILOA-linked reporting [6], and the primary planning page does not state a mass [5]. No LUT mass is stated in the primary paper [3]. LuSEE-Night has a strict mass limit with no figure given [4]. The RT-1 mass is not publicly specified in the sources read.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No instrument-level power figure was verified for any example. The LUT paper does not give a power value [3], and the Apollo 16 record does not give one [2]. The ILO-X planning page gives 200 W of solar power for the lander's surface operations. That is a lander value, not an instrument consumption [5]. LuSEE-Night is battery-powered, with no figure given [4]. Power requirements for RT-1 are not publicly specified in the sources read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface observatory must survive the lunar environment and operate within it. Thermal control is the main constraint in these examples. The ILO-X optics are designed for -180 degrees C to +70 degrees C [5]. The LUT CCD was cooled to -40 degrees C for science images [3]. According to a secondary source, the Apollo 16 camera was placed in the lunar module's shadow to limit heating and glare [10]. Lunar night, which lasts about two weeks, is the central survival challenge for solar-powered observatories, and the LuSEE-Night team identifies survival through it as the key open question [4]. Dust and vacuum affect optics and mechanisms. Data must be stored onboard or relayed: ILO-X carries 32 GB of onboard memory per imager [5], and LuSEE-Night's first dataset is expected to take about 40 days to reach Earth by relay satellite [4]. Pointing is also an operational constraint. Fixed imagers see only the sky region set by the lander's orientation [5], whereas LUT's gimbal allows tracking [3].
article.limitations: The main limitations are as follows. The payload name describes a class, so no single design can be specified. Lifetimes are short or uncertain: the Apollo 16 surface operation is reported as about three days in a secondary source [10], and the ILO-X planned surface life was nearly two weeks [5]. Fixed imagers have a field of view set by the lander's orientation [5]. Solar-powered systems must survive lunar night [4]. A surface observatory also depends on a single lander or rover, so a landing failure or an off-nominal orientation can remove it [6]. Finally, data latency can be long [4]. Several examples have only partial performance data, and their numbers cannot be compared directly [3][5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface observatory is a surface payload. Its transport chain covers Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing delivery, deployment, setup, and the power, data and thermal interfaces to the lander or rover. The examples differ. An astronaut set up the Apollo 16 camera [2]. Lunokhod 1 carried RT-1 on a rover [9]. The Chang'e-3 lander delivered LUT, which was launched on a Long March-3B rocket [3]. The ILO-X imagers were fixed to the IM-1 lander [5]. LuSEE-Night is planned for delivery by a commercial lunar lander, with its antennas deployed after touchdown [4].
transportation_process: Integrate the observatory with the lander or rover on Earth, including thermal, power and data interfaces, and any heater or shielding requirements (for example the LUT cooling and the ILO-X optics temperature range [3][5]).
Launch on the carrier rocket. The Chang'e-3 LUT launched on a Long March-3B rocket on 2 December 2013 [3].
Transfer to the Moon and deliver to the surface. The Chang'e-3 lander touched down two days before LUT's first light on 16 December 2013 [3].

Deploy. Methods differ: astronaut set-up for the Apollo 16 camera [2], rover-mounted instrument for RT-1 [9], fixed lander-mounted imagers for ILO-X [5], and antennas deployed from a turntable after the lander is powered down for LuSEE-Night [4].
Set up, check out and survive the lunar night. Relay the data through a satellite, which for LuSEE-Night is expected to take about 40 days for the first dataset [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Methods vary. The Apollo 16 camera was set up by astronaut John Young and was re-aimed during the stay, according to a secondary source [2][10]. RT-1 was mounted on the rover and pointed at the zenith [9]. The ILO-X imagers are fixed with no moving parts [5]. LuSEE-Night deploys its antennas from a turntable after touchdown [4]. LUT used a gimbal-mounted pointing mirror inside the telescope [3]. How the telescope itself was mounted to the Chang'e-3 lander is not described in the paper [3].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The historical examples discussed here are Lunokhod 1 RT-1 (1970) [9], the Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera (1972) [1][2], the Chang'e-3 LUT (2013) [3], the ILO-X imagers on IM-1 (2024) [5][6], and the planned LuSEE-Night radio observatory [4].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No verified interface document for a generic surface observatory was reviewed. The IM-1 flight carried the ILO-X imagers [5], and the LuSEE-Night carrier has been reported as Firefly's Blue Ghost lander [8], which has not been confirmed against an interface document. This article does not assert compatibility with any other named lander, rover or spacecraft.

article.historical_significance: Surface observatories are an early line of lunar astronomy. Lunokhod 1's RT-1 was an early attempt at X-ray observation from the lunar surface [9]. The Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera recorded the Large Magellanic Cloud from the lunar surface in April 1972, and its film transport mechanism was returned to Earth [1][2]. The authors of the Chang'e-3 LUT paper describe it as the first robotic astronomical telescope working on the lunar surface [3]. The ILO-X imagers and the planned LuSEE-Night antennas extend the approach to commercially delivered landers and to radio astronomy [4][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name lunar surface observatory describes a class of instruments rather than one specification, so this article does not give a single set of physical values. Evidence strength differs between examples. The Apollo 16 and Chang'e-3 LUT descriptions rest on primary or agency-linked records, but the Apollo 16 mass and focal-length values come from a secondary source [10], and the RT-1 specifications rest on a secondary summary [9]. The ILO-X aperture and mass rest on ILOA-linked reporting [6], and the LuSEE-Night frequency range and launch timing rest on secondary summaries [7][8] rather than on a current primary schedule. Operating status after the first weeks of ILO-X, and the present status of LUT and LuSEE-Night, were not confirmed. The scientific results of RT-1 and the detailed photometric and exospheric findings of LUT were not reviewed in full. This article does not recommend lunar landing sites, which the user has deferred.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file contain no query strings or fragments. No image assets were verified in this run, so no image objects are included.

data_quality_notes: Apollo 16 camera mass (22 kg) and focal length (75 mm) are from a secondary source [10]; not checked against NASA primary documents.
RT-1 mass, dimensions, power and scientific results are not verified in primary sources.
LUT limiting magnitude, mass, power and lander mounting are not stated in the primary paper [3]; current operating status not confirmed.
ILO-X aperture (3 cm) and mass (about 0.6 kg) are from ILOA-linked reporting [6]; post-landing operating status not confirmed.
LuSEE-Night launch date, carrier and frequency range are from secondary sources [7][8]; not confirmed against a current primary schedule.
Two source pages (BNL news, ILOA planning article) are identified by query parameters that the URL policy removes; the cleaned base URLs may not resolve to the cited article.
No image assets were verified from official pages in this run, so no images are placed in the article.
